en: The *Qiongjue Laoren Tianqi Zhizhu* (The Lone and Desolate Old Man Tianqi’s Direct Commentary on the Ancient Cases) by Master Tiantong Jue;
compiled by the Śramaṇa Xingfu of Ciren on the Golden Terrace.
The Later Scholar Śramaṇa Jingshen deeply reverently carved [this record] for the World-Honored One.

One day, the Master ascended the seat (directly revealing the truth at the center). Mañjuśrī struck the mallet and said (startling the assembly with a great function): "Observe clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King."
The Dharma King’s Dharma is thus (a full commentary). When the World-Honored One descended from his seat (seeing that something was leaked, he could not avoid sweeping away the traces).
○ (The main intent is directly revealed; the purport clarifies the Great Function. Summary (Master and disciple sing in harmony).

"A single segment of true wind—do you see it? (Every person is fully endowed with a single segment of true wind. The World-Honored One has personally presented it; Tiandong asks you all: do you see this true wind?)”

The eternal Mother of Transformation employs principle as her shuttle; she weaves an ancient brocade containing the imagery of spring. (The World-Honored One releases the harmonious breath of spring, and Mañjuśrī immediately causes the leaves to unfurl and the flowers to bloom.
These two are like warp and woof interlacing to weave a single brocade; this means that only when one acts as the head and the other acts as the tail is the whole completed.

Alas, what can be done about the Lord of the East’s leaking? (Mañjuśrī strikes the gavel and the World-Honored One descends from his seat. He knows only to sweep away the traces, unaware of the leakage; hence it is said, "Alas, what can be done.")

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty asked Master Bodhidharma, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? (He set aside both the conventional and the ultimate to directly inquire about the Middle Way, presenting his understanding to test the Master.
Dharma said, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. (There is not a single dharma to be found—how can one establish the Noble Truths?

One stroke, two cuts. The Emperor said, "Who is it that faces me? (Failing to grasp the essential point, he pursues the words back to their source. Dharma said, "I do not know. (A direct cut at the head, allowing no room for duality. The Emperor did not attain realization (the provisional and the real did not meet). He then crossed the river and departed.
Wei [Xuan] (The main theme grasps the essential sentiment; the purport clarifies the upward direction). Summary: (Failing to meet one who knows). "Vast and open, there is no sage.
The incoming stimulus is far removed from the ordinary (meaning they do not yield to one another, grasping directly).

Is this not like striking the nose with an axe? (The sacred truth is like the clay remaining on the tip of the nose; "vast openness" is like the axe striking the clay). Failing, one does not turn back, but falls into the rice steamer (the meaning does not accord, like a broken steamer).

Emperor Wu pursued him again as he ground [his stone], never looking back. He sat alone in the vast stillness; at Shaolin, he remained silent. This was the total upholding of the true command (it was not merely sitting in cold silence or remaining speechless).

This is the total upholding of the true command. The autumn is clear as the moon turns; the frosty wheel and the river are pale. The Dipper hangs down like the handle of night (Autumn’s clarity does not violate the present moment;

the turning moon does not violate that which is beyond kalpas. Directly pointing to the center, not a hair’s breadth remains. Thus it is said: "The Dipper hangs down like the handle of night"). The lineage of robes and bowls is entrusted to sons and grandsons;

from this point on, humanity and heaven become medicine and disease (The Patriarch presented his face directly, yet people still failed to grasp the meaning. To this day, they merely rely on oral transmission and mental reception, passing down the robes and bowls. Is this not shameful? Tiantong does not speak of this).
Emperor Wu deeply admonished those who would come after him.
The King of East India invited the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, for a vegetarian feast. The king asked, "Why do you not look at the scriptures?

(The Venerable One, in the midst of the assembly, directly showed the king his doubt; he sat in silence, not reciting. The Patriarch said, "This poor monk’s inhalation does not dwell within the realms of the aggregates. (He sat upright in stillness.)

The outgoing breath does not involve external conditions (clarifying that one does not sit in partiality; this commentary clarifies that the primary function should be directly revealed from the center).

Constantly turning such a sutra hundreds of thousands of millions of times through the mind (in and out without restriction, correct and partial being sovereign, not falling into existence or non-existence;

thus it is said "constantly turning"). ○ (The main intent is to be directly revealed from the center; the meaning is clear, with the pivot of the mechanism presented within the words. Summary (neither light nor darkness falls).

The cloud-rhinoceros plays with the moon, its brilliance radiating (not dwelling in the realm of darkness; it is revealed alone in the midst of obscurity). The wooden horse roams the spring, its swiftness unrestrained (not entangled in manifold conditions; in the midst of clarity, all marks are severed).
Beneath the brows are a pair of cold, azure eyes (the Venerable One’s two eyes were perfectly clear and bright, hence they are said to "contain the radiance" and be "unrestrained").

As for reading the sutras, how could one ever penetrate the ox-hide? (This disparages the great assembly who vainly bore into old paper; like eyes wrapped in leather, when will they ever break through? With a clear and enlightened mind, one transcends vast eons (the five aggregates...).
Emptiness (the heart’s void clarity manifests alone). The Heroic Power breaks through the heavy siege (the majesty of power moves freely within the realm).

The wondrous, perfect pivot turns the spiritual mechanism (the movement of the spirit pivots; left and right are unrestrained). Hanshan forgets the path by which he came (for ten years he has forgotten the way back;

this speaks of the monks who are deluded regarding themselves and pursue external conditions). Shide accompanies him, walking hand-in-hand home (Liu Qiu Yin met Shide and they entered the gate hand-in-hand; the Venerable One has returned neither to the King nor to the assembly).

The Honored One Smiles (The Great Function Deeply Appraised). (The Main Intent: The Probe Rod is Held in Hand; the Purpose is Clear: The Great Function is Personally Presented. Summary: (The Realized Ones Meet One Another.)
Boundless spring upon the tips of a hundred grasses; taken at random from the hand, its use is intimate (Indra takes it from his hand at will;

like spring covering the earth, there is no selection). The merit of the sixteen-foot golden body is gathered; casually taking hands, one enters the red dust (the World-Honored One’s compassionate heart; his entire body falls into the weeds).

Amidst the dust, he acts as the sovereign (the four immeasurable minds serve as the lords of the ten realms); Transforming all that lies beyond, he becomes a guest who comes of his own accord (the Way pervades the universe; who would not come to seek refuge?).
In this life of sensory contact, one is sufficient according to one's lot (the World-Honored One and Śakra both follow their respective portions);
one does not begrudge that one’s skills are not equal to others (one does not begrudge that my own virtue and conduct have not yet matched those of the world).
A monk asked Qingyuan, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? (He was seeking instruction. Qingyuan said, "What is the price of rice in Luling?
(A turning phrase that cuts through the body; the intent is clear, decisively severing the practitioner at the point of encounter. [General Summary: The claws and fangs of the Dharma cave.]

In an era of Great Peace, the administration of affairs leaves no outward sign (the four barbarian tribes do not invade and the myriad people enjoy their vocations; there is no merit or rank, so what sign could be shown?).

The rustic style of the village elders is most pure; they simply attend village songs and community feasts. Who knows of the virtue of Shun or the benevolence of Yao? (The Way of Yao and Shun is ultimate governance through non-action.

The village elders—people of the outskirts—know only of village songs and community feasts, unaware of the transformation of non-action. This says that those of Qingyuan eat when hungry and drink when thirsty, unaware of either the Buddha-dharma or worldly dharmas.)

A monk asked Mazu, "Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations—[namely: the proposition of existence, the proposition of non-existence, the proposition of both existence and non-existence, and the proposition of neither existence nor non-existence;
once these four are transcended, the hundred negations naturally cease]—I pray that you, Master, will directly point out the meaning of the Westward Transmission.
Mazu said, "Today I am weary and cannot explain it for you. Go ask Zhizang. The monk went to ask Zhizang. What did Zhizang say?
Without asking the Master [Zhao-yong Simultaneity]. The monk said, "The Master sent me to ask you. Zhao said, "I have a headache today and cannot explain it for you;
go ask my brother Hai. (This is like saying: "A son is not born without a father. The monk asked Hai. Hai said, "When I get here, I do not understand" (This is like saying:
"One knows only to exhaust the law, but does not care for the lack of subjects"). The monk brought up Mazu. Mazu said, "Zang’s head is white; Hai’s head..."
Black (Directly Pointing to the Center) ○ (The Main Intention Directly Pointed Out; the Principle is Clear and Beyond Reliance). Summary (The Scale and Weighing in Hand).
Medicine Causing Illness was Witnessed by the Sages of Old (Setting aside the medicines for the four continents, this monk becomes the illness as a reverse verification).

Illness Becoming the Physician—must it not be someone? (Exhaustion and headache are the illness of the world; father and son are the physicians. As for medicine acting upon illness, tell me, who is it? White-headed and black-headed alike—victory!

The sons of the house—Baitou Zhizang and Heitou Zhihai—both capable of upholding the lineage and able to bear its burden. As for "having a word" and "having no word," these are the devices for cutting off the stream (the Master and his son possessed words;

Vimalakīrti’s single silence was without words; in their application at that time, both cut off the stream). Standing tall, they sit and block the path of the tongue (the character *táng* means "clarity";
father and son have spoken). One should laugh at the old, ancient sage of Vaiśālī (one should laugh at him for holding fast rather than letting go).
Yaoshan had not ascended the seat for a long time. The head of the monastery said, "The assembly has long been longing for your instructions;
we pray that the Master will preach the Dharma for the sake of the community. Yaoshan ordered the bell to be struck. When the assembly had gathered, he ascended the seat.
After a long silence, he descended from the seat and returned to his quarters. The head followed him and asked, "Master..."

"Just now you promised to preach the Dharma for the assembly; why do you not utter a single word? (He did not realize he had lost his own ground, yet instead he resented that [the Master] would not speak.
The Mountain said, "The sutras have sutra masters; the treatises have treatise masters. Why blame the old monk? (A single point, two applications.
○ (The main intent is to show directly from the center; the principle clarifies the total presentation of great function. Summary (Pointing upward).

The foolish child’s deliberate money for silencing his crying (what comes out of the mouth and enters the ear is all yellow leaves used to stop a child's wailing; yet the foolish child treats them as real gold).

A fine steed chasing the wind turns its head at the shadow of the whip (when the outsider asked the Buddha about existence or non-existence, the World-Honored One remained silent for a long while; the outsider was greatly enlightened—this suggests that the patch-robed monks of this eastern land are not the equals of the outsiders from the West).

Clouds sweep the vast sky; the moon-nesting crane, its cold clarity piercing to the bone, cannot sleep. (Clouds sweep the vast sky and not a speck of dust remains; the moon is bright and the crane is white, a hundredfold.)
[The Master said,] "I understand. On the contrary, I am surprised that you do not speak; how could you possibly fall asleep?
One day, while Baizhang was ascending the hall to preach, there was always an old man listening to the Dharma. When the assembly had dispersed, the old man did not leave.
Baizhang asked, "Who is this person standing here? The old man replied, "In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I once lived on this mountain."
A student asked a man of great cultivation, "Does one who has reached such practice still fall within the realm of cause and effect? He replied, "One does not fall within cause and effect.
[Because he saw the Master’s hand surpassing the ordinary and transcending the conventional, the student abandoned his own view to follow him, making this request to be first and last.

Now I ask the Venerable Master to provide a turning word in his stead. Baizhang said, "Cause and effect are not obscured. [The former response dismissed them; the latter picks them up and turns them around, enabling the other to be immediately free from stagnation.]
[Emptiness and Non-existence]. Upon hearing the old man’s words, he attained great enlightenment (truly a man of brilliance who did not fail his purpose).
[The main theme shifts the pivot of the koan; the intent is clarified through the realization of the kōan. Summary: Attaining the intent by following conditions.
One foot of water, ten feet of waves (falsehoods lacking reality). For five hundred lifetimes prior, there was no way out (retribution is felt because of delusion).

"Neither falling nor being obscured"—this is a matter for deliberation. As before, one stumbles back into the thicket of complications (formerly two monks discussed this, saying: "If it does not fall, where does it descend? If it is not obscured, how can it be liberated?").

Such entanglements have not yet been completely eradicated; the intention must transcend the crowd. Before words or thoughts have emerged, it is said: "As before, one has run right back into it. A-he-he! Do you understand? (Tiantong speaks from the depths of his own breast, pointing directly at the core. He asks you all:
Is this laugh something that does not fall [into categories], or is it something that is not obscure? If you can understand it here, you will escape the frantic competition of the two extremes.

If you are truly free and untrammeled, (if you do not pursue the two extremes, you will naturally be relaxed and open), then it does not hinder my being boisterous and jovial. (This is like a baby learning to speak.)

Its appearance neither falls into conceptualization nor sinks into obscurity; it is entirely sovereign. First, both extremes are simultaneously stripped away so that neither remains; later, both are simultaneously granted freedom so that both may act as they please.

Divine songs and village dances form their own melodies; amidst them, one claps and chants "Lila. (If this is so, whether on this side or that, there is nothing acceptable and nothing unacceptable; one naturally follows conditions without discrimination.)
One day, two halls at Nanquan were disputing over a cat. Nanquan held up the cat and said, "If you can speak, I shall not kill it" (he casts his hook with the full power of his mechanism).

The assembly was speechless (he cuts them off without fail). Nanquan then cut the cat in two (neither ordinary nor sage remains). Nanquan raised this matter to ask Zhaozhou (he clears away the previous meaning).

Zhaozhou took off his sandals, put them on his head, and walked out (he personally presents the Great Function). Nanquan said, "My son, you have saved the cat" (he rewards virtue upon its manifestation).
○ (The main theme is casting the hook; the intent clarifies the Great Function. Summary: (Father and son sing in harmony.

The assembly of monks from both halls all scramble and struggle (arguing in confusion). Old Master Wang was able to test the orthodox and the heterodox (Old Wang held up a cat to distinguish the ordinary from the sage).

With a sharp blade he severed [all attachments], and both images were forgotten. For a thousand ages, people have loved this master of the school (fully raising the correct command; revered by all past and present).
This Way has not yet been lost; one who recognizes it is truly praiseworthy (having met a true connoisseur, the master’s craft is revealed).

To excavate the mountains and pierce the seas, he follows only in the footsteps of the Great Yu (the former assembly of monks blocked this Way; now the King-Old Man has reopened it, manifesting his divine function like that of the Great Yu alone).

To smelt stones and mend the heavens, he is uniquely worthy of Nüwa (seeing what was previously lost, the current great restoration is like that of Nüwa, only then attaining perfection). Old Zhaozhou has his livelihood—grass.
The tip of the shoe is slightly worn (these subtle points must not be many; they uniquely reveal that Zhaozhou possessed both hand and eye). Coming from amidst the different, he is a clear mirror;
this very gold does not mix with sand (gold differs from sand; Zhaozhou differs from the multitude).
On the road to Mount Tai there was an old woman. Whenever a monk asked, "Which way does one go for the road to Mount Tai?

(the question being an ordinary inquiry), the woman would say, "Go straight ahead. (She pointed directly toward the center. As soon as the monk had taken a step (realizing he had strayed from the correct path), the woman would say, "What a fine master! (a master who knows how to lose his way).

Again, he went off like that (a missed opportunity). The monk reported this to Zhaozhou (he raised it because he had doubts). Zhaozhou said, "Wait, let me investigate this" (he must hear the matter; he has not yet seen its core).
Zhaozhou asked, "Where does the path to Mount Tai lead? (holding the probe in hand). The woman said, "Go straight ahead" (pointing directly at him face-to-face).
Zhaozhou then walked away (falling for the trap). The woman said, "What a fine master, yet he goes off like that" (she spoke only to point him out, unaware—).
[The Master] ascended the hall of the prefecture and said: "I have thoroughly investigated and exposed this old woman for you (one presentation, one hook).
[This is the main intent and skillful means for the sake of others; the principle is clear, yet they fall into traps and views. [This concludes the section on the heart's fortune.]
"An old woman who has attained the essence—her transmission is unerring. (The old woman was truly capable of benefiting others; I praise her for having attained the essence.

"Zhaozhou, the Ancient Buddha, succeeded Nanquan" (Nanquan’s disciple; a renowned master under heaven). "Carving the tortoise costs it its life because of the image" (Pointing out that the old woman had her eyes changed by Zhaozhou, like a tortoise whose entrails were carved out).

"A fine steed chasing the wind is repeatedly entangled by the tether" (Pointing out that Zhaozhou was pulled and led by the old woman, like King Mu’s horse 'Chasing the Wind' which could not avoid being restrained by the halter). Investigation.
Broken (do not boast of your mastery). This is the "Wife’s Zen" (do not show off your cleverness). To speak of it before others is not worth a penny (the two of you need not flaunt your brilliance).
[This] has all been seen through by the Celestial Youth).
Master Yunmen said: "When light does not penetrate through, there are two kinds of illness (the heading).

To be unclear in all places, with something standing before one—this is the first [illness] (the numinous light is mixed with objects; because light and object are not distinguished, it is called 'unclear'). When one penetrates so that all phenomena are empty, it remains indistinctly present."

It seems as though there were some kind of thing; this too is because the light has not been fully penetrated (the numinous light emerges from existence yet mingles with non-existence; it appears to possess awareness, yet one cannot realize its non-existence).

Therefore it is said: "Deeply hidden. Furthermore, the Dharma-body also has two kinds of illnesses (heading). Upon attaining the Dharma-body, one fails to forget the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

One’s own views still persist; one has fallen into the side of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This is because, having transcended the previous [dichotomy of] existence and non-existence, one suddenly realizes the Dharma-body and clings to it without letting go—therefore, one's own views remain.

Even if you manage to penetrate through this, you must not let it pass (if you do not let go of the Dharma-body, you will dwell in great effort; if you shed it and become without reliance, you will again dwell in effortless mastery).

Examine this closely: what breath of life is there? It is also a sickness. (If you dwell in effortless mastery, even that effortless mastery is a sickness; you must further examine it. Suddenly, when you see through it, it is all one scene.)
(An object for laughter) ○ (The main theme: seizing the essence to shatter attachments; the intent is clear—there is no falling into stages. Summary: (The grandmotherly heart is urgent.
The myriad phenomena of the universe stand towering and majestic. To penetrate through them is boundless, yet nothing obstructs the eye. (Directly clarify the source. Heaven and earth are all here;

yet those who wish to be liberated are instead hindered by external objects. Who has the power to sweep away this gateway? Hidden within the breast, it naturally forms its own sentiment. (Who can clear it away?)

All things are now realized as true emptiness (yet this is merely the hidden man giving rise to a view of emptiness). The boat lies across the wild crossing, immersed in autumnal azure; The oars enter the reeds, reflecting the brilliance of snow.

An old fisherman with embroidered robes yearns for his former market; Drifting on a single leaf, he sails upon the crests of the waves. (The boat is moored in dead water, forever unable to move—this is attaining the Dharma-body while clinging to it and refusing to let go. (The oars turn the prow back into the reeds—this is not abiding in the Dharma-body, yet sitting in pure clarity.
(The embroidery is torn into a single color; the fisherman is broken in dead water; the market is broken at the solitary peak.)
This clarifies the turning of the position according to its function (the "lowering of the hand").
Dìzhàng asked Xiū Shānzhǔ, "Where have you come from? (turning toward the event, [Dìzhàng] uses the "peak"). Xiū said, "From the South. (Directly providing.
Dìzhàng said, "How is the Buddha-dharma in the South these days? (Hiding the point. Xiū said, "They are engaged in vast debates. (Directly providing. Dìzhàng said, "How can it compare to..."
"I am planting fields here to grow food for my meals. (If it were like this, it would not be as good as planting fields. Xiu said, "What can you do about the Three Realms?
(If you are only seeking food to eat, how will you escape the Three Realms? Zang said, "What do you call the 'Three Realms'? (Seeing him running outside, he gave him a pull by the nose.
(Main Idea: The probe is held in hand; the intent is revealed through the words. General Summary: The scales are held in hand.
